egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-meat-ma.title: Egg Omelet with Meat Cooked with Cooking Spray

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet with meat prepared using cooking spray is a quick dish that became popular in the early 1990s. Eggs are beaten, pieces of cooked pork are added, and the mixture is cooked in a pan sprayed with a non‑fat cooking spray, reducing added fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish emerged in the United States in the early 1990s when cooking sprays entered the mass market.
The spray allows cooking without oil while preserving the flavor and texture of the meat.
The omelet is often served with toast, fresh vegetables, or mashed potatoes.
Variations include cheese, herbs, onions, or bell peppers.
Its fast preparation makes it popular among students and busy professionals.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs and pork provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and overall tissue maintenance.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Both eggs and meat supply B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Low added fat
items.content: Using cooking spray instead of oil reduces the amount of saturated fat in the dish.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Pork contributes iron and zinc, important for immune function and blood formation.

items.title: Satiety
items.content: The combination of protein and a small amount of fat helps keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium in spray
items.content: Cooking sprays often contain salt; people monitoring sodium intake should use them sparingly.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use fresh or properly stored pork to avoid the risk of foodborne illness.

items.title: Egg freshness
items.content: Eggs should be fresh; older eggs can harbor salmonella.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs contain cholesterol; individuals with high cholesterol should limit consumption.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, cut into portions. It pairs well with whole‑grain toast, fresh vegetables, avocado, or a light sauce. Optional toppings include grated cheese, herbs, or hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat in a dry pan or microwave to retain texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Trout is a freshwater fish of the salmon family, inhabiting rivers and lakes in temperate climates. In Russia and CIS countries it is often labeled “NFS” (New Freshness), highlighting its clean taste and high nutrient content. Trout has delicate pink flesh, a moderately fatty flavor, and a characteristic aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trout can change sex during its lifetime depending on environmental conditions.
Unlike many salmonids, trout usually does not migrate to the ocean and lives its whole life in fresh water.
The largest recorded trout weighed over 20 kg, though typical specimens are 1–3 kg.
Trout is widely farmed in aquaculture where water temperature is kept at 10‑16 °C for optimal flavor.
In Japan, trout is often prepared as “sabay” – a smoked‑salty delicacy.

items.title: Rich in omega‑3
items.content: Trout provides EPA and DHA – polyunsaturated fatty acids that support heart and brain health.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: 100 g of trout delivers about 20 g of complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Trout is a good source of B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish contains selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, supporting immunity, bone health, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low mercury content
items.content: Compared with large oceanic predators, trout has minimal levels of heavy metals.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including trout.

items.title: Parasite contamination
items.content: Raw or undercooked trout can harbor parasites; cooking to an internal temperature of 63 °C is recommended.

items.title: Sodium in smoked trout
items.content: Smoked trout often contains added salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Environmental considerations
items.content: Improper aquaculture practices can lead to water pollution and antibiotic use.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Trout can be grilled, baked, boiled, or pan‑fried. It is commonly served with lemon, herbs (dill, parsley) and a light sauce. Smoked trout is used in salads, sandwiches, and appetizers. Raw trout (sashimi) is popular in Japanese cuisine but requires strict quality control.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh trout should be kept in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic film or an airtight container, and used within 2 days. Frozen trout can be stored at –18 °C for up to 6 months. Before cooking, check the smell: the fish should have a fresh, mild scent without ammonia notes.

potato-mashed-from-fresh-made-with-milk.title: Mashed Potato from Fresh, Made with Milk

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potato made from fresh potatoes and milk is a smooth, creamy side dish. The potatoes are boiled until tender, then mashed and blended with milk, butter, and optionally seasoned with salt and pepper.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the most widely consumed root vegetables worldwide.
Traditional mash is often made from yellow or white potatoes, which have a lower starch content than red varieties.
Adding milk creates a lighter texture and a subtle dairy flavor.
In many cuisines, cream, butter, or cheese are added for extra richness.
Mashed potatoes serve as a base for casseroles and dishes like shepherd's pie.

items.title: Rich in potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which helps maintain normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, supporting immune health and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The starch in potatoes offers a steady release of energy.

items.title: Betaine content
items.content: Betaine in potatoes supports liver function and homocysteine metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from milk
items.content: Milk adds calcium and, when fortified, vitamin D, which are important for bone health.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so portion control is advised for diabetics.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Excessive salt added during preparation can increase sodium intake, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food safety
items.content: If cooked potatoes are left at room temperature too long, bacteria may grow and cause foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Top with fried onions, fresh herbs, grated cheese, or garlic for extra flavor. For a lighter version, use low‑fat milk.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftover mash in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Reheat with a splash of milk or cream to restore creaminess. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though texture may become slightly watery after thawing.

content.title: About
content.content: The whole wheat hamburger bun (item 2513) is made from whole grain wheat flour, contains bran and seeds, making it more nutritious than standard white buns. It has a soft yet sturdy crumb, a subtle nutty aroma, and a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole grain buns retain more fiber, B‑vitamins, and minerals than their white counterparts.
The bran content aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.
Added seeds such as sunflower or pumpkin increase healthy fat content and give a richer flavor.
Historically, whole grain rolls have been favored in European cuisines as a “healthier” bread option.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports regular bowel movements, helps regulate blood sugar, and contributes to prolonged satiety.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole wheat provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: The bun supplies magnesium, iron, and zinc, important for muscle function, blood formation, and immunity.

items.title: Lower glycemic impact
items.content: Compared with white buns, whole wheat releases glucose more slowly, aiding blood‑sugar control.

items.title: Healthy fats from seeds
items.content: Seeds add polyunsaturated fatty acids that are beneficial for heart health.

items.title: Grain allergy
items.content: People with wheat or gluten allergy may experience reactions and should avoid this product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some versions contain added salt; individuals monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: While more nutritious, the bun still provides calories; moderation is key for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Perfect for building hamburgers, sandwiches, and open‑face toast. Toast lightly for a crisp crust, then add lettuce, tomato, cheese, and sauces. Also works well as a side for soups or as a base for appetizers.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a cool, dry place in an airtight bag or container. For longer shelf life, store in the refrigerator to prevent drying out and mold growth. Discard if mold or off‑odors appear.

salisbury-steak-with-gravy-potatoes-vege.title: Salisbury Steak with Gravy, Potatoes, Vegetables (Frozen Meal)

content.title: About
content.content: Salisbury steak with gravy is a ready‑to‑heat frozen meal that includes a seasoned beef patty in a savory gravy, boiled potatoes, and a mixed vegetable medley. It is designed for quick preparation in a microwave or on the stovetop, delivering a complete meal in just a few minutes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was first introduced in the United States in the 1950s as a convenient home‑style dinner.
Salisbury steak is named after Dr. James H. Salisbury, an early 20th‑century physician who promoted the recipe for its nutritional value.
Typical ingredients include ground beef, onion, carrot, and seasonings, with a gravy made from beef broth and tomato paste.
Modern frozen versions retain flavor through rapid blast‑freezing technology.
Each package is usually a single serving (about 300‑350 g).

items.title: Protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and vegetables supply B6 and B12 vitamins, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potatoes are a good source of potassium, which helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Dietary Fiber
items.content: The vegetable mix adds fiber, promoting healthy digestion.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: Sodium Content
items.content: Prepared frozen meals often contain added salt; individuals with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: To extend shelf life, some products include food preservatives that may not be suitable for everyone.

items.title: Beef Allergy
items.content: Although rare, some people may be allergic to beef or to seasoning ingredients.

items.title: Heating Requirements
items.content: Insufficient heating can leave live bacteria; follow the recommended time and temperature guidelines.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Remove the meal from its packaging, heat in the microwave or on the stovetop until the internal temperature reaches at least 75 °C (167 °F). Serve immediately; garnish with fresh herbs or a splash of sauce if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen meal at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. Once opened, consume within 24 hours if stored in the refrigerator. Discard if you notice off‑odors or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Sesame (Sesamum indicum) seeds are tiny oily seeds that come in white, golden, and black. They have a nutty, slightly sweet flavor that comes out especially after toasting. Sesame is sprinkled on buns, salads, and dishes, and is made into tahini, halva, oil, and the paste for hummus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sesame is one of the oldest oilseed crops.
Sesame is made into tahini, halva, and sesame oil.
The phrase open sesame is linked to the way ripe sesame pods burst open and scatter their seeds.
Black sesame usually has its hull and contains more calcium, while white sesame is more often hulled.
Sesame is widely used in Asian, Middle Eastern, and Mediterranean cuisines.

items.title: Contains calcium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals are needed for bones, muscles, and nerves.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support oxygen transport and immunity.

items.title: Contains lignans
items.content: Sesamin and sesamolin are compounds with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Contains healthy fats
items.content: Most of the fat in sesame is mono- and polyunsaturated.

items.title: Source of protein and fiber
items.content: Sesame provides plant protein and fiber, especially when unhulled.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Sesame is recognized as a major food allergen, and allergy to it can be severe.

items.title: High in calories
items.content: Sesame is high in calories, so portions should be small.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Sesame contains oxalates, which people prone to kidney stones may need to limit.

items.title: Whole seeds
items.content: Whole seeds may be poorly digested; it is better to chew them well or use them ground or as tahini.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: To bring out the flavor, lightly toast sesame in a dry pan until golden. Sprinkle it on buns, salads, vegetables, rice, and noodles, add it to dough, or make it into tahini, hummus, gomashio, and sauces. Small amounts are best.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store sesame in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long-term storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer, because the oils can turn rancid. After opening, store tahini in a cool place or in the refrigerator. Discard seeds that smell rancid.

content.title: About
content.content: Textured vegetable protein (TVP), dry, is a defatted soy protein obtained from soybeans. It has a porous, meat‑like texture and is used as a meat substitute in vegetarian and vegan dishes. TVP has a neutral flavor, allowing it to absorb the taste of sauces and seasonings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: TVP is produced by extrusion, where soy protein is forced through a die under high pressure and temperature.
It is often called “soy meat” or “soy chunks.”
Dry TVP has a long shelf life – up to 2 years when stored in a dry place.
It contains about 50 % protein and virtually no fat, making it popular among athletes.
TVP rehydrates quickly in water or broth within 5‑10 minutes.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: TVP provides roughly 50 % protein by dry weight, supporting muscle maintenance and satiety.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: It contains almost no saturated fat, suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Soy protein is rich in these trace minerals important for immunity and metabolism.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber in TVP promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Supports vegetarian and vegan diets
items.content: A complete plant‑based protein source without animal products.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People allergic to soy may experience reactions ranging from mild to anaphylaxis when consuming TVP.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; combine TVP with vitamin C‑rich foods to mitigate this.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMO)
items.content: Most soy crops are GMO; choose non‑GMO certified products if required.

items.title: Sodium in seasoned varieties
items.content: Some flavored TVP mixes contain added salt; check labels if monitoring sodium intake.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Before cooking, soak dry TVP in hot water or broth for 5‑10 minutes, then drain. Use it in stews, sauces, veggie burgers, tacos, chili, or add to casseroles. Its neutral taste lets it take on any seasoning or sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry TVP in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For extended storage, keep it in the refrigerator or freezer to prevent moisture absorption and quality loss.

vegetable-and-fruit-juice-100-juice-with.title: Vegetable and Fruit Juice, 100% Juice, High Vitamin C

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetable and fruit juice is a 100% natural juice made from a blend of fresh vegetables and fruits. It contains a wide range of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, with an especially high vitamin C content (4903 mg per litre), making it an excellent way to support the immune system.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The juice is produced without added sugar, preservatives, or artificial flavors.
Combining vegetables and fruits provides a broader nutrient profile than single‑fruit juices.
Vitamin C remains stable thanks to cold‑pressing and rapid pasteurization.
The juice is often used in sports nutrition for faster post‑workout recovery.
Its high acidity can enhance iron absorption from plant‑based foods.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C is a powerful antioxidant that supports immune function and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Hydration support
items.content: With over 90% water content, the juice helps maintain the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium supports normal heart and muscle function and helps regulate blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phytonutrients from the vegetables and fruits help neutralize free radicals.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Natural dietary fiber in the juice promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity may cause discomfort for people with gastritis or acid reflux.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: The blend may contain fruits or vegetables that trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Although no sugar is added, natural fruit sugars can raise the glycemic index.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Large doses of vitamin C may affect the efficacy of certain drugs, such as anticoagulants.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink the juice chilled in small servings throughout the day. It can be added to smoothies, used as a base for cocktails, or drizzled over salads for extra flavor and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in its original container. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Discard if the colour, smell, or taste changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Vodka and soda is a simple cocktail made of plain vodka diluted with carbonated water (soda). The drink has a light, refreshing taste, moderate strength, and is often served in tall glasses over ice.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The vodka‑soda combination originated in the United States in the early 1920s as a lighter alternative to straight vodka.
Vodka and soda is frequently used as a base for more complex cocktails such as the Vodka Tonic or Vodka Spritz.
Carbonated water helps soften the perception of alcohol on the palate, making the drink more “drinkable.”
In some countries it is served as a “shot‑cocktail,” where a shot of vodka is chased with soda.
Soda can be plain or flavored (lemon, lime, grapefruit), altering the flavor profile of the drink.

items.title: Moderate consumption
items.content: When consumed in moderation (1‑2 servings per week) vodka and soda can provide relaxation without a large calorie load.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Carbonated water contributes to overall fluid intake, especially when the drink is made without added sugar.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Unlike many mixed drinks, vodka and soda contains virtually no sugar, making it a better choice for those monitoring blood glucose.

items.title: Alcohol intoxication
items.content: Vodka is a high‑proof spirit; even when diluted it can cause intoxication and associated risks.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Carbonated water may increase bloating or discomfort in people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Alcohol can amplify the effects of certain medications; limit intake when taking drugs.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: Pour 40‑50 ml of vodka into a tall glass over ice, add 150‑200 ml of cold soda water, stir gently. Optionally garnish with a lemon or lime wedge.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store vodka in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. Use fresh soda water, and keep opened soda bottles refrigerated and consumed within 2‑3 days.
